name: DDoS and Traffic Filtering
intent: Why a flood is stopped at different layers depending on its kind, why blocking IPs fails against distributed or spoofed sources, and what every filter costs the legitimate users it misjudges.
scenario: A service handles 200 legitimate requests per tick: 60 home users with their own IP and one office of 40 people behind a single NAT address. A toy tick simulation hits it with a volumetric flood, a SYN flood and an HTTP flood, and tries seven defences against each.
problem: A distributed denial of service attack does not break in; it uses up something finite: link bandwidth, the table of half-open connections, or application capacity. Each resource is exhausted at a different layer, so each needs a different defence, and a defence that works on one kind can be useless or harmful on another. Meanwhile the traffic is easy to mistake for a busy day, the attacking addresses are many, spoofed or shared with real users, and every filter is a guess about who is legitimate.

howItWorks.title: Three kinds of flood, three resources
howItWorks.text: A volumetric flood (UDP amplification, reflection) tries to fill the link, measured in bits per second. A protocol flood such as a SYN flood fills a state table, measured in packets per second: each spoofed SYN makes the server keep a half-open entry while it retransmits the SYN-ACK (up to about a minute with Linux defaults). An application-layer flood sends valid requests from real clients, such as expensive searches or login attempts, and exhausts CPU, database or connection capacity at a request rate that looks modest in bandwidth terms.

howItWorks.title: Volumetric: it must be absorbed before your link
howItWorks.text: Once a 1,000 unit link is offered 5,200 units, it drops traffic indiscriminately, so legitimate traffic shares the same lottery: in the toy 19% of legitimate requests get through. Any filter behind the link, a firewall or a blocklist, sees only what survived. The defence has to sit upstream: anycast spreads one address over many sites so each absorbs a slice of the flood, and scrubbing there drops what matches the attack signature. Here 8 sites of 1,000 units, with toy scrubbing that removes 95% of the flood and wrongly drops 2% of real traffic, serve 98% of legitimate traffic. It still has a ceiling: at double the attack size the edge saturates too and service falls to 78%.

howItWorks.title: SYN flood: do not keep state for strangers
howItWorks.text: A SYN flood with spoofed source addresses fills the 1,024 entry half-open table, and legitimate SYNs find it full: 6% of legitimate requests get through. SYN cookies (RFC 4987) encode the connection details in the SYN-ACK sequence number and keep no state until a valid ACK returns; spoofed senders never answer, so they cost nothing: 100% served. Edge proxies that complete handshakes themselves have the same effect. Blocking IPs does nothing, since every spoofed packet has a fresh source.

howItWorks.title: Application floods: valid requests are the hard case
howItWorks.text: 500 real bot IPs sending 4 requests each is 2,000 requests per tick against 600 capacity, and legitimate requests are crowded out proportionally: 27% get through. Each bot is individually modest, so nothing in the packet or the IP stands out. The defences that can work are behavioural: a challenge (a proof of work, a script a browser runs, a CAPTCHA) that most bots fail, and request-level limits on expensive routes. In the toy a challenge passed by 95% of users and 10% of bots (made-up pass rates; real ones vary widely) restores 95% of legitimate traffic.

howItWorks.title: Why blocking by IP fails
howItWorks.text: With spoofed sources there is no real address to block. With a botnet, there are thousands of addresses each below any sensible limit. And the biggest sender is often the legitimate one: the office behind a NAT sends 80 requests from one IP while each bot sends 4. Blocking the 10 busiest IPs removes the office and 9 bots: legitimate traffic served falls from 27% to 17% while the attack barely changes. A per-IP limit of 3 also makes things worse (22% served), because each bot stays under it and the office is cut to 3 requests.

howItWorks.title: Every filter costs legitimate users something
howItWorks.text: A filter is a classifier with false positives. The challenge in the toy loses 5% of real users; edge scrubbing loses 2%; a per-IP limit of 1 loses 69% of real requests and still lets 492 attack requests per tick through. The question for each defence is not whether it stops the attack but what it costs the people you want to serve, and whether it can be switched on only while the attack is happening. Rate limiting and load shedding are the generic safety valves, but they protect the service, not the fairness between users and attackers.

pros: Anycast and scrubbing absorb volumetric floods that no single origin link could survive
SYN cookies and edge handshake proxies make SYN floods nearly free to ignore
Challenges and behavioural checks separate bots from people without relying on IP addresses
Layered defences let each layer stop the kind of traffic it can actually identify
cons: Every filter has false positives, and the cost lands on real users, often the ones behind shared NAT addresses
Capacity-based defences have a ceiling: a bigger flood saturates the edge as well
Application-layer floods look like real traffic, so detection is probabilistic and arms-race driven
Always-on scrubbing and challenges add cost and latency during the long stretches without an attack
whenToUse: Putting a CDN or DDoS protection service in front of public endpoints so volumetric traffic never reaches your origin
Enabling SYN cookies (typically already on by default in common operating systems) and sensible half-open limits
Per-route rate limits and cheap-first checks on expensive endpoints such as search, login and checkout
Challenges and shedding policies that switch on under attack, with a way to switch them off again
whenNotToUse: Relying on blocklists of IP addresses as the main defence against distributed or spoofed traffic
Applying very tight per-IP limits without accounting for NAT and carrier-grade NAT, where thousands of users share an address
Hiding the origin address and assuming that is enough: it needs to be unreachable except through the edge
Building bespoke scrubbing for volumetric attacks: capacity at that scale is bought, not built
pitfalls: Filtering behind a saturated link: the filter sees only the survivors, so legitimate traffic is already lost
Blocking the busiest IPs: the busiest address is often a legitimate office, school or mobile carrier behind NAT
A per-IP rate limit that bots sit under: 500 bots at 4 requests each pass a limit of 5 and still send 2,000 requests per tick
Origin exposed: if attackers can find the origin IP they bypass the edge entirely
Challenges that lock out API clients, search crawlers and accessibility tools
Leaving emergency rules on after the attack: the false positives continue indefinitely
Not rehearsing: without a runbook and known capacity numbers the team improvises under pressure

roles.label: Legitimate users
roles.description: Home users with their own IP and an office behind one shared NAT address.

roles.label: Attack traffic
roles.description: Floods of packets, spoofed SYNs or valid requests from a botnet.

roles.label: Edge network
roles.description: Anycast sites with scrubbing, handshake proxies and challenges, in front of the origin.

roles.label: Origin
roles.description: The service with its link, half-open connection table and request capacity.

quiz.question: A flood fills your internet link so that 80% of all packets are dropped, legitimate ones included. Where must the defence sit?
options: Upstream of the link, at the edge, so the flood never reaches your link
In the firewall on the origin server, with a larger blocklist
In the application, with per-user rate limits
In the database, with more connections allowed
quiz.explanation: Anything behind a saturated link only sees what survives. The traffic has to be absorbed or filtered before it consumes your bandwidth: anycast and scrubbing at the edge.

quiz.question: An application-layer flood comes from 500 real IP addresses, each sending 4 valid requests per tick. You block the 10 busiest IPs. What most likely happens?
options: The attack stops because the top senders are bots
The attack drops by about half
Nothing changes, because the attackers switch to spoofed addresses
You block a legitimate shared NAT address and the attack hardly changes
quiz.explanation: Each bot is modest, so the busiest addresses are usually legitimate large senders such as an office behind NAT. Blocking 10 of 500 bots barely dents the flood while real users lose service.

quiz.question: A SYN flood with random spoofed sources fills the half-open connection table. Which defence is directly effective?
options: A per-IP rate limit of 3 requests per tick
A CAPTCHA on the login page
A blocklist of the 10 busiest source addresses
SYN cookies, which keep no state until a valid ACK arrives
quiz.explanation: Spoofed senders never complete the handshake, so a server that stores nothing until the final ACK is unaffected. IP-based limits do not work on random spoofed sources, and a CAPTCHA acts at the application layer, after the handshake.
